I. THE MEASURES.

1. Preface.

The Ebers Papyrus is available to everyone through the publication we have produced.¹) On account of its thoroughly correct orthography, it has hitherto rendered the most important services to the grammarian, who cannot do without it as soon as he turns to the study of Old Egyptian as opposed to what is called New Egyptian in the papyri of the XIX. and XX. Dynasties. For cultural history and the history of medicine, its contents are likewise of great interest and have been widely used; however, the physician has hitherto known little what to make of the proposed remedies, or has passed over the fragmentary translations of individual recipes, not least because many of the prescribed drugs had to remain unidentified and nothing at all was established regarding the measures by which they were to be taken. The absurdities, too, which the papyrus contains at individual passages, and which people were far more inclined to bring forward than the good material of which it is full, deterred him. We therefore set ourselves the task of treating this fine manuscript in such a way that non-Egyptologists, physicians, naturalists, and philologists of every kind might form an accurate picture of it; and on the whole it is of such a nature that it does credit to its author, when we consider the circumstances under which he composed it.

1) Papyrus Ebers, preserved in the University Library at Leipzig. A hieratic handbook of ancient Egyptian medicine. Edited, with an introduction and translation of the diseases contained therein, by Georg Ebers. With the support of the Royal Saxon Ministry of Culture and Public Education. Leipzig. W. Engelmann 1875.

Whoever wishes to connect their own work to our research using means other than the tools of our specialized discipline may do so with confidence, guided by what is offered here; for we follow the method of not transcribing any word we do not understand with complete certainty, but of transcribing the entire text in a consistent manner and providing it with a thorough commentary beneath the text.

In this way we intend later to treat the entire manuscript, but first to extend our method only to one of the most important sections of the papyrus — the one devoted to eye diseases.

Already through Herodotus we learn that specialization among Egyptian physicians was carried out with particular strictness. The oculist was permitted to treat only ailments of the sense of sight and no others, and the eye doctors of the Nile enjoyed the highest esteem among the other peoples of antiquity. Egypt is even today a favored breeding ground and place of observation for eye diseases. To learn more about these and their treatment by the Egyptians is a matter close to the hearts of many of our ophthalmologists, and several of them approached the author with inquiries and the request to open up the understanding of the papyrus to them. Thus we chose the chapter devoted to eye ailments in order to test our method on it and to offer physicians, linguists, and friends of the history of medicine a reliable foundation for their own study.

Regarding the papyrus itself, its origin, the time of its composition, etc., we have said what was necessary in the preface to our publication of the manuscript,²) and what has been accomplished in this field of research between the completion of that work and the present day has only confirmed our fundamental views and added little that is new to what was remarked in the preface to Pap. Ebers.

Our manuscript is the hermetic book on medicinal remedies (περὶ φαρμάκων) mentioned by Clement of Alexandria,³) it

It was certainly written during the reign of the XVIII Dynasty, at the latest around 1500 B.C.; it is a compilation, in which very ancient⁴) and some foreign⁵) prescriptions were included, and the measurement signs, which appear alongside the names of the proposed medications, refer partly to volumetric measures and partly to weights.

2. The Transliteration.

The method of transliteration, which we employed in accordance with Prof. Dr. L. Stern in the preface to the publication, possessed certain advantages, in that it partly aligned with the system agreed upon at the Orientalist Congress in London (1874) in consultation with our advisory board, and partly made it possible to recognize whether the scribe employed alphabetic or syllabic signs. To be sure, the transcription is thereby burdened with many diacritical marks, whose typesetting causes inconveniences; moreover, it has not found acceptance, and gradually most colleagues have also departed from the London method. The liveliest objection arose against the transliteration of those signs that were regarded as vowels, and it is indeed problematic to call vowels those signs to which a consonantal value originally certainly belonged. Nevertheless, it is advisable to retain our Latin letters, if one does not wish — and there is much to be said against this as well — to use the unforgettable Charas of the Coptic alphabet⁶); for the hooks ị, ȝ, which G. Steindorff proposed using in his excellent dissertation, present difficulties, and yield in their application—

4) Pap. Ebers, LXVI, 15—18. A hair-growth remedy for the lady Šeš, mother of King Tâ.

In France, Maspero has in recent times departed considerably from the London method, particularly in the transcription of vowels. To be sure, he knows how to support his own system convincingly in various ways, but he might perhaps be willing to compromise, if another new system were on the verge of being generally adopted.

mixed with Roman characters, creates an unpleasant sight for the typographer's eye, and beyond that they do not even render significantly better service than Roman letters furnished with appropriate diacritical marks for the transcription of certain sounds.⁷)

In transcription, the first priority is that it allow one to recognize easily and reliably which characters of the original it represents. In the second place, since it cannot avoid the use of dashes and hooks, it should cause the typesetter as little difficulty as possible and not be outright painful to the eye. If it meets these requirements, the third desideratum will also be easily fulfilled: that it be acceptable to as many scholars as possible and comprehensible to those outside Egyptological research circles as well.

The sign ⸗ᵃ represents, as many Semitic names transcribed with hieroglyphs teach us, the Hebrew ע. It is therefore by no means our "a" or any vowel at all; and yet I do not hesitate to transcribe it as a, since this indicates just as reliably as ‹ that the original is ⸗ᵃ, and moreover many Semitists transcribe ע as a. Non-Orientalists must be warned not to take the ‹ for the Greek spiritus asper and the › for the spiritus lenis. What matters most is a clear, unmistakable rendering of the base script; very little depends on the form of the signs, as long as they can be written and printed conveniently. Using the transcription to do justice to the history of individual sounds and to indicate the value they originally possessed is not feasible, or at least leads to an overloading that makes printing more difficult, more expensive, and more—

We could sooner subscribe to this system, although 𓇋 and ⸗ᵃ do not at all suit us, and good reasons can be brought against 𓅱 == w, for which much can be said. Unfortunately, knowledge of this method came to us too late for us to make use of it in what follows. Later we may perhaps adopt it in general, but certainly in the transcription of consonants, since, for example, ḥ suits us better than χ for ☉, and d̠ appeals to us more than t for 𓌀.

This method of transcription also has the advantage that it connects, where possible, to the familiar characters of Lepsius's standard alphabet that are available in printing houses. Not a single letter would need to be newly cast; for the ȧ, which is easily composed from a and ', is in any case for the trans-

script of Semitic texts is in use; the e with the puncta diareseos is absent from no typesetter's case, and even if we do not conceal from ourselves that the Greek χ and ϑ, with which we transcribe ☉ and ⟹, are somewhat foreign among the other Roman letters, we nonetheless leave them untouched; for even though ch and th suffice for Germans, these letters would lead other language communities to a pronunciation that might deviate from ours and from that of the Egyptians. Elsewhere we have already dealt extensively with the reasons that prevent us from transcribing ⟹ as d, and it does not by any means express a purely medial sound; yet we submitted to the transcription warmly recommended by Erman and adopted by several colleagues. The t for ⌐ produces in print an image that is anything but attractive, yet we preferred it to d, because the latter is just as much a conventionally formed sign as t, and t became established in printshops and among specialists through the standard alphabet and the London transcription method of 1874. Its true pronunciation will have been close to the English th, and for such a sound a t is a more appropriate basis than a d.

For the Semitist, we place beside the letters of the transcription the corresponding letters of the Hebrew alphabet. With regard to the consonants this can be done with some confidence, since we possess a fairly large number of Semitic names and loanwords that were transcribed by the Egyptians in hieroglyphic texts using their alphabet, and which allow us to recognize which Egyptian sounds the hierogrammist equated with the Semitic ones. The vowels present greater difficulty, yet ꜣ regularly corresponds to א and \_\_ (which is of course not a vowel) to ע. For ꜣꜣ the sign ' most frequently appears. ן and ☉ were used by the Egyptians to transcribe the Hebrew ׳, and we would have preferred to render it as w rather than u, had not the plural endings and similar considerations determined us to retain the old u. Much has been disputed about the w. L. Stern and A. Erman devoted particular attention to it, and I believe I may count on the agreement of both when I transcribe it as e.

3. The Determinative Signs.

Whoever has familiarized himself with our transcription alphabet will be able to grasp easily and precisely the phonetic value of any text rendered with its help; yet hieroglyphic writing also offers an explanatory and illustrative element that makes it easier to determine the meaning of many words, especially those denoting concrete objects. We refer to the so-called determinative signs. These are placed after the phonetically written word and indicate to which conceptual category it belongs. Names belonging to the plant kingdom are determined with ꜥꜣ, or, if they denote trees, with () or ⊕. After the names of drinks and liquids appears the image of a hollow vessel ©, ⊕ or ∞, and after those of quadrupeds a piece of their hide with the tail ꜣ.

It is easy to understand what great and welcome assistance these signs provide precisely for determining the conceptual value of words that denote remedies or body parts proposed for treatment. We therefore consider it necessary to make these important aids accessible to non-Egyptologists as well, and for this reason we place after the name of each medicament its determinative.

The group △ △ ꜣ will therefore be transcribed not merely as gngn-t, but as gngn-t ꜣ, in order to show the reader that the word written gngn-t must be counted among the vegetable kingdom — with the exception of trees, which have their own class sign. The very frequent ⌓₁₁₁ © ⊕ we transcribe not as prt ùan, but as prt ₁₁₁ ùan © ⊕, from which it becomes apparent that prt ₁₁₁ represents something in the form of a grain (grain, seed, berry), while ùan © ⊕ represents a tree — specifically, on account of the ©, a tree with fragrant parts or parts traded commercially. From the addition of both determinatives the reader can immediately recognize that the entire group denotes the seed or one of the other products designated by ₁₁₁ of a tree that has a

By this method we also make independent research easier for the non-Egyptologist; yet, in order to avoid misunderstanding, we feel compelled to clarify that we by no means wish to see this system adopted universally, nor applied to the transcription of historical, religious, or narrative texts. There it would burden the transliteration, whereas for the understanding of our prescriptions — which are composed entirely of real substances — the inclusion of the class-sign accompanying the name of each medicament is strongly recommended.

In the list that follows, one finds the most common determinatives along with an indication of their meaning. The so-called "direct" ones explain themselves; for they are identical to the image of the object which the word — before or in place of which they appear — conveys to the mind. The group can, for example, only mean a pig; for this is placed beyond doubt by the direct determinative, the image of a pig, which follows the word še, which, like the Upper Egyptian Coptic ero, means pig.

4. The Measures.

1. Method.

The measures present particular difficulty, and in order to establish the signs relating to them, it is not sufficient to measure the existing weights and dry measures and to determine which name occurring in the texts refers to each one; rather, the method requires here above all proceeding from recipe to recipe,

to go from drug to drug and first to compile all the measures which the papyrus prescribes for use. After this, one must examine which measures are to be regarded as measures of volume, which as measures of weight, and only then will one be able to establish the weight or content of the individual measures and the value of the fractional signs, which prescribe taking so and so many parts of a unit. Finally, the prescriptions of the entire papyrus must again be examined, in order to test the correctness of the results obtained and to decide whether certain signs and numbers in a particular position might mean something special.

2. The Specific Measures of the Papyrus.

There are four measures which the Egyptian physician uses most frequently. For all weighings, one and the same unit is used everywhere and without exception. It breaks down into fractions which we shall have to examine more closely, yet the name of this so extensively used apothecary weight is mentioned nowhere. Among the measures of volume there are 3 which are to be regarded as properly calibrated measures, and of these only two are subdivided into parts. The most frequently occurring is the measure written hieratically as ꞁ, which probably corresponds to the hieroglyphic dnat ꞓ and with which ordinarily only liquid substances are measured, as well as the apothecary measure ꞓ Re or Ro, which is mentioned at no point in the papyrus, but which seems to us certainly and indeed quite frequently to be intended. Parts of these two volume measures are also prescribed, while the third is ordered only in full quantities²⁴). It is called hnu ȿ, hnu ȿ, hn (hin), corresponds in name to the Hebrew הִין and is not to be distinguished from the hnu that appears alongside it. In favor of the identity of both measures speaks especially the prescription LIV, 14–16, which calls for 1 hnu honey, 1 hnu²⁵) beef fat, 2 hnu liquid

The unit of weight, as we firmly believe, is correctly calculated by Hultsch at 6.06⅔ grams; 1/16 of this would represent only a fraction of a berry, as we found from weighing grapes that we had prepared for us at the Schellenberg pharmacy in Wiesbaden by the obliging gentlemen provisors. It is, however, difficult to believe that a small piece of grape was added to the medicament. On the contrary, these prescriptions are best explained if we connect špt ☉ (the Coptic ϭⲉⲙ means only "to shear") with the ancient Egyptian root šp, which denotes giving off a liquid, spitting it out and pouring it. H. Brugsch rightly derives from the same root the word šp, used in our papyrus for "blind," špu or šup, which originally means having run out, dripped from the eye. Our špt ☉ must therefore — and the determinative does not contradict this — be understood as the droplet-like discharge of the grape and the gum tree. We therefore translate šept nt ʽerr as grape juice, špt ☉ nt qnyt as gum drops, and we will have hit upon the correct meaning.

18. We do not enumerate the cakes and types of bread with which the drugs are to be mixed or into which the medications are to be shaped, although these also relate to the form of the prescribed remedies. XI, 1 and 2, for example, require that the proposed substances be made into a šns bread and eaten. XLVII, 4 includes a hât flatbread of the same bread type among the medications. The ordinary bread is proposed as a medicament, to be weighed and measured.

Extraordinarily varied are the vessels that were used in the Egyptian pharmacy, and this certainly attests to the refined development of pharmacy in ancient Egypt. Among them belong, as mentioned, the measures of capacity already noted above: the Hin and the dnât.

19. The Hin or Ḥnu. LXV, 14 states that the medication is to be placed in a hnu (Hin-jug); a new Hin-jug is mentioned several times; LXXX, 16 states that the remedy is to be placed in a new Hin-jug; XLIX, 20 states that the woman etc. is to drink the remedy from a Hnu-jug; indeed, the material of the jug itself is proposed as a medicament: LXIII, 8 and XCIV, 12. 4. Definite Weights and Hollow Measures.

a. Items to be taken by the piece and their number.

If we now turn to the determination of the measures by which the prescribed medicaments are to be partly weighed and partly measured, we must here recall the method which strictly forbids drawing conclusions from individual statements, while it imperiously demands that in each individual case the entire manuscript be kept in view and allowed — with particular regard to the measures — to explain itself by itself.

§. b. Weighing.

Once all the prescriptions have been consulted, it is easy to distinguish what is to be measured by volume from what is to be weighed, even though the unit of weight and one of the most frequently used volumetric measures are never mentioned by name.

For everything to be weighed, only one weight is used, whose unit is not named; its subdivision, however, follows the same system throughout. In the introduction to Pap. Ebers, p. 48, we proposed to connect this medicinal weight with the later Arabic dirhem or the drachma, and to equate the unit used by the author of the papyrus with the double drachma, which weighed approximately 6.220 grams. Later studies led us away from this view, and it now seems certain to us that in the unit in question we should recognize a weight which was connected with the system of [hieroglyph] udn [hieroglyph] or [hieroglyph] udn, as P. Bortolotti³⁵) cleverly demonstrated, and which was meant to equal in weight the cube of the smaller cubit. We see this used everywhere when precious metals are to be weighed; and alongside it the [hieroglyph] qt, which linguistically corresponds to the Coptic ϪΤ as the drachma and weighed one tenth of a udn [hieroglyph]. But this Qt [hieroglyph] of 9.096 grams would be too heavy for us to accept as the unit of our papyrus, and so we agree with Hultsch³⁶) when he identifies ²/₃ of the Qt as this unit, which would then have amounted to 6.064 grams, a weight not too far removed from our first determination³⁷), according to which it would have weighed 6.220 grams.

4, c. γ. The Ro.

The measure Ro has already appeared to us as the smallest part of the bše divided into 320 parts in the mathematical Papyrus Rhind, and we have noted that, although it is never named there, it also occurs in our papyrus. We will now have to substantiate this. Its — that is, the Ro's — use in the hermetic book that compiles the remedies of Egyptian medicine — for that is what the Pap. Ebers is — was to be expected from the outset. The knowledge of prescriptions of the Egyptians, for whose refined development our manuscript provides such brilliant testimony, did not remain the exclusive property of the physicians active on the Nile; rather, it was observed from them by learned Greek physicians in Alexandria and transferred into the pharmacological science of the Hellenes. And even though it has not yet been very long since

that European and above all English scholars of distinction attempted to demonstrate that the Greek scholars who worked in Alexandria as members of the Museum or independently, following a new method and achieving great things especially in the natural sciences, mathematics, and mechanics, did so entirely uninfluenced by their native Egyptian colleagues, without looking around in their immediate vicinity, and far from borrowing anything whatsoever from the Egyptians, relying entirely on themselves and arriving from within themselves at the astonishing advances of which their writings are full — they will now find themselves compelled to abandon this opinion, which they defended with erudition and polemical skill but little discernment. The well-known tenderness for the originality of the Greek mind, which in their view would have suffered had it not remained free from all foreign influence in every area of its activity, had led them to regard the Hellenes — whose open gaze looks out at us brightly and attentively from their works — as dull and short-sighted; for that is what they would have been, had they in fact closed their eyes to the stores of knowledge of the Egyptians accumulated in their immediate vicinity, whether due to an inability to learn a foreign language, or out of fear or reluctance to borrow anything from a barbarian people. But do we not hear frequently enough of interpreters or hermeneutai, who from the beginning of the XXVI Dynasty, from Psamtik I onward into Roman times, were to be found everywhere along the Nile as intermediaries between Egyptians and Hellenes? Do we not know that in Hellenistic Egypt, from the first Ptolemies onward, Greek was the common spoken language among native Egyptians, and was understood and spoken by everyone, and certainly by scholars as well? And as for what lies behind that supposed "reluctance," this is further shown by the admiration, heightened to the point of exaggeration, that leading figures of intellectual life in Greece — from Thales, the head of the early Ionian school, through Pythagoras and Plato, down to comparatively late times — devoted to Egyptian wisdom. Yet even if none of these tributes had come down to us, the specialized research of recent times in the fields of mathematics and metrology would teach us that,

6. Where weighing or measuring is to be done.

From what has been said it follows that where whole numbers appear without the addition of a specific unit-sign, these ordinarily indicate the ratio of the individual drugs to one another. A prescription in which the stroke 1 — that is, the numeral one — stands after the name of every suggested ingredient is to be taken in equal parts. The quantity normally taken of an individual drug was equal to the Ro of 1.41 centiliters. Only after the last substance in the list of drugs in a prescription — the binding agent — did the stroke acquire, as we shall show below, a generally different meaning. When very small doses were involved, one made use of the 64 parts of the drachma-weight of 6.064 grams. When in a prescription whole numbers exceeding one appeared alongside the numeral one, it was ordinarily only the proportion in which the individual ingredients were to be taken that was being indicated. If in the same prescription, as in LXII, 22 — LXIII, 1, there were whole numbers and fractions belonging to the system of weights, then as a rule all drugs were to be weighed. 11. The Various Meanings of the Same Sign.

From this it follows that some signs were capable of a double interpretation; yet this could safely be left to the experience of the apothecary. He knew in advance what the binding agent was to be, and could furthermore recognize it from its position at the end of the prescription. A glance at the series of prescribed drugs and the instruction following their enumeration as to how they were to be prepared and applied taught him whether the fraction after the binding agent referred to the Ro or the dnat, and the stroke to the Ro or the Hin.

When ½ is prescribed without further specification of the measure, it can be understood as half of the dnat, the Ro, or our drachm; and the same applies to ¼, even though this fraction most frequently belongs to the weight system. ⅓ and ⅔ can only determine how much of the Ro or dnat is required. The fractions mentioned relate to the latter, however, only when the sign 𓏲 accompanies them, or when they appear after the name of a binding agent at the end of the prescription. The unit, the stroke |, usually refers to the Ro, but after the binding agent at the conclusion of the prescription it sometimes also refers to the Hin.

Thus all the occurring measure signs would be accounted for, and it remains only for us to investigate how 𓌀 and ⟹ differ from one another, of which we know that both mean ½.

Moreover, no smaller portion than ¼ of the Ro is prescribed, and we see no way to determine the measure we have identified as 1 Ro other than as it has been done. In the numerous recipes in which the names of all drugs are followed by the stroke |, and which are therefore to be taken in equal parts, neither the dnât 7 nor the Hin ℌ can be conceived of as a unit; the drachm also hardly comes into question, certainly not for those remedies that are to be taken in ⅓, ⅔, and ¾ portions. For recipes to be prepared in equal parts, both the dnât 7 and the Hin ℌ would be far too large, and alongside them a much smaller hollow measure must certainly have been used, one that was divided according to the duodecimal system and preferably into thirds. This could never under any circumstances refer to the drachm weight, because the latter breaks down only into fractions whose numerators are 1 and whose denominators are powers of 2. Thus the Ro, whose name is mentioned just as rarely as that of the drachm weight, will rightly receive the value that we assigned to it after considering all its occurrences throughout the papyrus.

There are quite a few of these, as our dear colleague, the excellent mineralogist Professor F. Zinkel, informs us, even apart from verdigris, which does not occur as a mineral. Phosphorchalcite, Libethenite, Tagilite, the water-containing arsenic-acid copper minerals Olivenite, Euchroite, Strahlerz, the water-containing sulfuric-acid copper mineral Brochantite, and the water-poor vanadium-acid limestone copper Volborthite were probably not in the hands of the ancients, all of which are green. Present in antiquity were Malachite, i.e. basic carbonate of copper, and water-containing siliceous copper. This too was green, and it seems as though scarcely anything else could be meant by ueta. One can hardly think of Malachite or verdigris; for although the latter is frequently mentioned, and a few small antiques made of this mineral have survived (e.g. a pile-dwelling statuette in Dresden), its name msfkt ° never alternates with our ueta °, although this certainly means "that which is green." Verdigris was found in tombs, but it certainly did not need to be imported from abroad. Used adjectivally, uet serves to designate the green color of the sea, of crops, and of artworks on which the green color has been preserved. On the Sinai Peninsula were the mines from which the Egyptians obtained Malachite, which was also frequently brought to them as tribute by Asiatic peoples, and the ueta-mineral; for this (determined with [sign], and thereby designated as stone), is named as a product of the land of Bẓ, i.e. of Petraic Arabia and later also of Persia. The water-containing siliceous copper could have had the same homeland, was green and fulfilled the conditions we must require of the uetu. We therefore consider ourselves justified in naming it Siliceous Copper, i.e. water-containing silicic-acid copper, though with a † as a mark of critical caution.

In the 18th Dynasty it is mentioned among the drugs which the fleet of Hatshepsut brought to Egypt from Punt (Arabia Felix or the Somali coast). Dümichen, Fleet of an Egyptian Queen, p. 2. It was used as a salve par excellence, and in the linguistic form [hieratic signs] stm [hieratic signs] it served during the time of the writing of our Papyrus (18th Dynasty) to designate ointment and anointing in general. Later the same word was used, since most ointments contained stibium, to designate this mineral, which in Coptic S. is стнм, B. соnм, and which corresponds to stimmi or stibi, which according to Pliny hist. nat. 33, 101, along with alabastrum and larbasis, was the Egyptian name for antimony. The Greek στίμμις was also identified by Eustathius in his commentary on the Odyssey as an Egyptian word: καὶ τὴν μέλαιναν στίμμιν ὀμματογράφον, also the black eye-coloring Stimmis. According to Pliny it is a type of stibnite, which is burned or dried and powdered, to blacken the edges of the eyes with it. On this coloring see Virchow's "Old Egyptian Eye-black." Proceedings of the Berlin Society for Anthropology, Ethnology etc., 26 May 1888 and later my remarks ibid. 1889, p. 574 ff. In Dioscorides v. 99 ed. Kühn, all the properties of this metal are enumerated, where it is called στίμμι. It was also called πλατυόφθαιμον, λάρβασον, γυναικεῖον, the feminine, and χαλκηδόνιον⁷⁷ᵃ). Among other things it served to remove impurities and sores or lesions (ἕλκος = ulcus) and to cleanse the eyes. "In general its effect is similar to burnt lead." This note is important; for it appears that in Egypt, where stibium or antimony was hard to obtain, people procured a good eye-black by heating coal with lead sulfate. Indeed, in Azmim in Upper Egypt, small pouches of eye-black have been found with some mummies; these, a fine powder, were kindly analyzed for us by the famous successor of Liebig, Prof. von Baeyer in Munich. Plutarch's claim that the Egyptian priests disdained the onion because it stimulates thirst must rest on a misunderstanding, for one sees it far too often lying as an offered vegetable on altars. In Hern's instructive work "Cultivated Plants and Domestic Animals," p. 327 ff., the introduction of the citron into Europe is placed too late; for Herr in Zurich found citron seeds already in early Etruscan graves. In Egypt it was probably known early; and among the plants and fruits depicted by Thutmosis III, 18th Dynasty, at Karnak (Mariette XXX), one is probably our citron. Theophrastus's description, dating from the time of Alexander, of the Median or Persian apple IV, 4, 2 is well known. Virgil, Georgica III, 126, calls it "felix." — In any case the citron was already among the remedies proposed by Dioscorides (1st century A.D.). He calls it μηδικόν scil. μῆλον, κεδρόμηλον and in Latin κίτρια (citria) and assumes its general familiarity. His description leaves no doubt that the citron is meant. This text, as can be gathered from lines 14 and 15, was to be read aloud during the preparation of the remedy to be applied: tortoise brain mixed with honey. Similar passages appear at LIX, 3–4 and 6, and Plutarch, who in his work on Isis and Osiris is often well informed, recounts in Chapter 81 that passages from the sacred writings were read aloud to the ointment makers while they mixed the drugs that formed the incense known as Kyphi. The passage cited here refers to a mythological event, most probably the battle of Rā against Set-Typhon and his companions. The conflict is introduced by a storm in the night. In such a storm, one imagines Set in battle with Horus or, as here, with Rā Harmachis. In the process, the sacred column — the pillar upon which the image of Osiris, carved in mummy form, is mounted — falls into the water; that is to say, Osiris, on whose behalf the battle is being fought, disappears into his element, or, as the myth teaches elsewhere, into the underworld. Now the companions of Rā swing their staffs; for mnāt undoubtedly also means the prop or the stake, and is the same as the Arabic nabbût, the strong and long wooden staff in the hand of the Rhafire, the leader, etc., which serves simultaneously as a support and a weapon and which we also frequently encounter on ancient Egyptian images. We find it in the hands of various gods in place of the scepter, as well as in the hands of sailors who assist in the hunting of crocodiles, etc., of local overseers, supervisors, etc. In the battle there is a tremendous beheading. The heads fall into the water; yet the god knows how to catch them (ân) like fish and to replace them on the wounded. This cutting off of heads is something very common. The enemies of the good gods also frequently lose their heads in the Book of the Dead, and hsq tp sen, the cutting off of their heads (Book of the Dead, 49, 3) is a formula well known to Egyptologists. The visitor to the royal tombs of Thebes also encounters on the tomb walls, in scenes depicting life in the underworld, no small number of figures standing on their heads or feet with their heads cut off. But the reattachment of the heads also occurs on several occasions. After the battle between Set and Horus, the latter strikes Isis, who had

By means of a horse-hair threaded through a needle, the pterygion (Eg. crocodile or crocodile-jaw) is sawn away from the cornea; others, however, cut it off with the pterygotome. There are passages that quite decidedly forbid us to continue equating bādê ⟺ = Gerontoxon; for first of all, LIX, 22 proposes a remedy against the tšft-t ͦ₁₁₁ in the eye, which we take to be φλεγμόνη and thus a malignant eye inflammation, inasmuch as we connect tšft-t ͦ₁₁₁ with the Coptic ϩⲟⲣϫⲉϥ fervor, ardere, fervere. The same treatment is therefore prescribed for this and for tšft-t ͦ₁₁₁. The principal ingredient in the two proposed prescriptions is, however, as we shall see at LIX, 22, castor-oil leaves, and Dioscorides IV, 161 (164) prescribes these against the two eye diseases for which we take bādê ⟺ and tšft ͦ₁₁₁ to stand, namely against οἰδήματα = Chemosis and φλεγμόνης. We shall return to this in the commentary on the principal remedy against the tšft ͦ₁₁₁ disease.

LX, 19 finally contains an incantation that is to be spoken over a remedy against cataract, and in this incantation the healing substances are invoked which are intended to drive away the discharge of pus and blood from the hetu ⟺ disease, the bdê ⟺ (here instead of bādê ⟺), blindness or dimness of sight (špt ⟺), bleary eyes, etc. All these eye conditions are placed on an equal footing with bdê ⟺, and this is sufficient to refute the view that bādê ⟺ is the Gerontoxon. This eye condition, also called arcus senilis or the old man's arc, designates a white and sometimes yellowish circular line on the cornea close to its edge, based on fatty degeneration; it occurs commonly in elderly people and is harmless, even when a cataract incision is made through it. But bādê must be a very serious disease; otherwise it would not be mentioned in the incantation LX, 17 ff. alongside the other most grievous afflictions that the remedy is meant to cure, about which the formula is to be pronounced. Pantophthalmia (panophthalmitis) or even blenorrhea could be considered, names which the ancients did not yet know. Perhaps for them chemosis was the "Egyptian" eye disease. Since the Coptic name for Egypt, "χηme," originally meant "the black," from it were also derived χημεία, χυμεία, that is, the black or Egyptian art (our "chemistry"). A very similar formation could underlie the Greek χήμωσις for the relevant eye disease, which one would then have to translate as "the Egyptian one." The eye disease bâdê <=, which as we saw above is described as severe through the incantation Pap. Eb. LX, 20, is for us the chemosis, alongside which stands the malignant inflammation to be healed in our manuscript and in Dioscorides with castor-oil leaves, here called φλεγμόνη = φλόγωσις and there ℓℓft °₁₁₁ κοηζεφ, that is, the burning or glowing one. We therefore take bâdê <= to mean chemosis, which must be thought of as involving pus, and ℓℓft as a severe inflammation. Given the purely external method of observation of the Egyptian physicians and of Dioscorides, a more precise determination cannot be made. What the papyrus otherwise says about these conditions teaches only that against bâdê <= and ℓℓft °₁₁₁ the same remedy — castor-oil leaves with plastic clay and honey — was used, and that bâdê <= in any case belonged to the most severe ailments. The Met-stone or Haematite.

The [hieratic] met □ stone is also called at LXXXVIII, 17 [hieratic] med □ n'anχ [hieratic] — the Med-stone of Life or of mirror-metal? Its identification presents great difficulties. At LVII, 42 we encounter a plant [hieratic], for which at XLIX, 14 the variant [hieratic] met [hieratic] appears, and our stone [hieratic] and this plant thus share the same name. We recognized in the former the Chelidonium majus, while Stern held it to be the crocus, Coptic метλⲏ, ⲙⲉⲑⲗⲓⲟ. From both plants a yellow dye is obtained, and Dioscorides mentions the one as well as the other. Of the sap of Chelidonium maj. he says it is χροκώδης, that is, saffron-colored or bright yellow, and if we now look among the stones which he recommends as medicines, there is one whose finest variety must likewise have had the crocus or bright yellow color. "The best," he says, "appears to be that which has a saffron-like hue." Furthermore it is supposed to be easily ground, and the met □ stone is prescribed at our passage as well as at LX, 13 and LXXII, 3 to be ground and ground "fine." It is repeatedly used against eye diseases, and the same holds for the crocus-colored stone which Dioscorides V, 144 (145) calls σχιστὸς λίθος, and which according to him is supposed to be very effective against fatty degeneration of the eyelids and staphylomata (berry-tumors or grape-eyes). This schistus stone is our red glass-head, colored red iron ore, bloodstone, lapis haematitis, fer oligiste rouge fibreux, fibrous red iron-ore. The finer the needles into which one splits the stalactitic, grape-like mass of the stone, the more the red color of the iron oxide comes to the fore in them. From the stone related to Pap. Eb. The Egyptian year was divided into three seasons (Tetramenies) of four months each¹¹⁶). The Pert-season mentioned here, denoted ≋, means literally the season of coming out, of emerging, of sprouting (of the seed). In Egypt this occurred during our wintertime, and the Greeks were therefore correct when they translated the Pert-season as χειμών, winter. On the tablet of Tanis (Decree

they mention it among the products of the balsam shrubs, of which the ointment- and perfume-makers made exclusive use. In Brugsch's Dictionary, ser. IV 86, 5 that it has a very fine fragrance, and moreover that it has the color of hr ds stone or hr sd stone, in which Lepsius (Metals p. 128) recognized mountain quartz, which occurs milk-white but also red. The māmiāmā resin, whose name is also nfd ° |||, must not be confused with the doum palm meme, at Dendera mememe.

Those were therefore right who, disregarding the meaning of "pr," simply translated this tetrameny as the winter season. According to the Julian calendar it falls from November 17 to March 16. The Greeks naturally first became acquainted with the Egyptian months in Alexandria and other Lower Egyptian cities and therefore rendered their names in the Lower Egyptian form. Those belonging to the Pr-t ⊙ season are called Tebi, Mechir, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi. The remedy that follows is therefore prescribed for the period from the third month of the season of Sprouting (Phamenoth) to the fourth month (Pharmuthi) of the same tetrameny, which appears to signify the time from January 17 to February 16. If the fourth winter month were to be included, one could use the prescription until March 16. If we translate the prescription into our way of thinking, and hear that some remedy is to be taken from January to February, we would naturally first refer this to the days from January 4 to February 4; to include the second month would already be arbitrary; it must therefore in our case be assumed to cover the time from January 17 to February 16, even if an extension of this period might have brought the patient neither benefit nor harm.

It is the same rare survival of the Ganoids or enamel-scaled fish, which had played a great role in earlier periods of prehistory, but are now extinct except for a few genera, including the sturgeon. Our fish is rarer in the middle and lower Nile, more common in the upper. "It is also a beautiful fish, adorned with armor of diamond-shaped, enamel-hard scales, so that it can and must be the 'piscis loricata,' the sight of which delights the glorified dead. As regards the lung as well, this fits. The swim bladder of the fish is generally regarded as homologous to the lung of our vertebrates, which the ancient Egyptians had already recognized. Now in Polypterus this swim bladder is more lung-like than in other fishes, in that it is double and does not open, as the swim bladder normally does in fishes, into the upper cavity, but rather into the abdominal cavity. It also burrows into the mud, like the true lungfishes (Protopterus annectens from tropical Africa), and lives there during the dry season, during which that swim bladder might perhaps serve it as a lung. This would of course require a spongy structure and a rich blood supply, which still remains to be investigated. Lobart, Recueil View eg 1886, VII p. 101 ff., seeks in a compelling manner to demonstrate that we should see in the bq or qb-tree the Myrobalan, Moringa oleifera, known in German as "Oil-Moringa." This tree, common in Egypt, was also known to the ancients. According to Pliny, its oil appeared red in Egypt, green in Arabia, and had a pleasant fragrance. Lobart would have done better to name the tree he had in mind moringa aptera or guillandina moringa L.; this is the βάλανος αἰγυπτία of the Greeks, whose seed was used in pharmacies as nuces Behen and supplied ben oil, which is still used today in the preparation of fragrant oils and ointments. Leunis, Botany p. 459, counts the ben oil prepared from the kernel of guillandina moringa among the "most excellent fats." Our bq ∩ may well be the βάλανος αἰγυπτία of Theophrastus, who describes the tree well. Hist. plant. IV, 2, 1. It is the βάλανος μυρεψική of Dioscorides, whose name "acorn belonging to fragrant oil" already indicates the purpose it served. We would therefore like to regard our Bq-tree as guillandina moringa L., the Oil-Moringa, and the juice from its fruits as the ben oil of the pharmacists.

Instead of bedbugs, ancient medicine seems to have preferred bat blood, as in our papyrus, to smear on the places from which hairs were pulled out in cases of trichiasis. In the edition of the Collectio Salernitana prepared by Renzi, Naples 1856, Vol. IV p. 28, the following prescription by an ancient medical poet is cited¹⁷³):

On preventing plucked hairs from growing back again.
That hairs may not grow back again in any place, anoint with
The juice of verbena mixed with the blood
Of a bat.

Here we have, therefore, certainly the blood of the bat prescribed for trichiasis as well. That of the bedbug we do not find in our manuscript. For the scientific therapy of our time it may indeed be quite irrelevant which kind of blood is meant. Our prescription orders a surgical intervention: the pulling out of the hairs. If the papyrus contains no other surgical instructions, this by no means proves that the Egyptians were unaware of such things. Our manuscript is simply the hermetic book of medicaments. The one concerning surgery, or more precisely surgical instruments, περὶ ὀργάνων, which Clement of Alexandria also mentions, has unfortunately not yet been rediscovered. In it, many eye operations would likely be found recorded.
